I've been farming this land in Quzhou for over thirty years. My father farmed it before me. I know this ground — the sandy loam, the shallow water table, the dry springs. I don't need to think too hard about what to plant. There's really only one system that makes sense here: winter wheat in the cold half of the year, summer maize after the harvest. That's what my neighbors do, that's what I do. We rotate these two crops on the same 10 mu every year.

For the wheat, I'll plant in mid-October. I'll use the improved Jimai variety — the seed station in town sells it, the county ag office pushed it, and my yields have been decent. I'm not going to try anything fancy. I'll rotary till before planting, apply base fertilizer, then topdress at jointing. Three irrigations: one at sowing because the soil will be dry, one at jointing, one at heading. Two sprays for aphids and powdery mildew, usually May. I'll aim for around 450 jin per mu — that's what I've been getting.

After the wheat combine comes through in June, I'll plant maize directly into the stubble. No-till saves me time and fuel, and the summer rains usually carry the crop. I use Xianyu 335 hybrid seed — it's expensive but the yield is reliable. I'll only irrigate once, maybe at tasseling if August is dry. Two pesticide passes for stem borer and fall armyworm.

My son is in Shijiazhuang now. I manage this myself with some hired help at harvest. I keep it simple because I have to.
